title: The Dry Season: When God Feels Absent
subtitle: There is a kind of suffering the church almost never names, the slow draining away of the felt presence of God, the prayers that hit the ceiling, the Scriptures that have gone flat, the worship you go through while feeling nothing. What John of the Cross, Ignatius, and the long Christian tradition saw about spiritual dryness, why the silence is often not absence, and how faith learns to stand when feeling has gone.

connections.label: The Anxious Mind: Faith and Mental Health
Suffering and the Silence of God
Identity and Worth: Who You Actually Are

parts.title: The Prayers That Hit the Ceiling
parts.body:
There was a time it was not like this. You remember it, which makes the present harder. You remember when prayer felt like talking to someone who was there, when a verse could stop you cold and bring tears, when worship on a Sunday morning carried you somewhere and you came home full. You did not have to manufacture any of it. The presence was simply there, the way warmth is there in a sunlit room, and you assumed it would always be there because you did not know it could leave.

And then, slowly or all at once, it went. Now you pray and the words go up and nothing comes down. The ceiling is just a ceiling. You open the Bible that used to burn and the page is gray, the words are true and you believe them and they do not reach you, like reading a letter from someone you love in a language you have forgotten how to feel. You sing the songs in church and your mouth moves and your heart is a stone. You are not in rebellion. You have not walked away. You are doing everything you did before, and the One you are doing it toward has gone quiet, and you do not know why.

The worst part is the loneliness of it, because you cannot say it out loud. In the world you live in, a Christian who admits that God feels absent is a Christian who looks like he is losing his faith, and so you have learned to perform a closeness you do not feel. You testify to a presence on Sunday that you cannot find on Wednesday. You answer how are you doing spiritually with words that were true last year. And underneath it all runs the question that keeps you up, the question you would never ask in a small group, what if the silence is not a season but a verdict, what if he stopped speaking because I am not really his, what if the emptiness is just the truth finally showing through.

Let me say this carefully and at the start, because you need to hear it before anything else. The felt presence of God and the actual presence of God are not the same thing, and the difference between them is the most important lesson the dry season has to teach. You can be held by someone you cannot feel. A child asleep in a dark room is no less in his father's house because he cannot see him. The withdrawal of the feeling is not the withdrawal of the God, and many of the people who have loved God most deeply in the history of the church walked for years, sometimes decades, through exactly the desert you are in now, and came out the far side not with their faith destroyed but with their faith finally purified of everything that was only ever feeling.

And one more honesty, because this matters and the church gets it wrong constantly. Not every dry season is a spiritual gift. Sometimes the flatness is not God withdrawing to deepen your faith. Sometimes it is exhaustion. Sometimes it is grief that has not been grieved. Sometimes it is depression, a real illness that flattens everything including prayer, and that no amount of spiritual effort will lift because it is not finally a spiritual problem but a medical one. Part of the wisdom of the dry season is learning to tell which kind you are in, and there is no shame, none, in discovering that what you needed was not more discipline but rest, or a friend, or a doctor. We will get to how to tell the difference. But first you have to know that you are not alone, and you are not faithless, and the silence is not the verdict you fear it is.

parts.title: Why the Church's Silence About the Silence Is Dangerous
parts.body:
We have built a Christianity that runs almost entirely on feeling, and then we wonder why it collapses the moment the feeling stops. Modern Western faith, especially in its more enthusiastic forms, has trained people to measure their standing with God by their emotional weather, to take the warm sense of his presence as proof and its absence as alarm. We sing songs engineered to produce a feeling and call the feeling worship. We chase the experience and assume that the experience is the point. And so we have raised generations of believers who have no theology of dryness at all, who hit the first real desert and have no map, no name for what is happening, and no community that will tell them it is normal.

This matters because the silence is coming for nearly everyone, sooner or later, and a faith with no theology of absence is a faith waiting to break. The believer who has been told, implicitly, that real Christians feel close to God, will read his own dry season as failure or as fraud. He will redouble his effort, chase the old feeling, try harder to manufacture what cannot be manufactured, and when it does not come he will slide toward one of two cliffs. He will conclude that he has done something wrong, that the silence is punishment, and sink into a guilt that is entirely undeserved. Or he will conclude that the whole thing was never real, that the warmth he once felt was just emotion and now that it is gone the truth is showing through, and he will quietly walk away, not because he was argued out of his faith but because his faith was built on a feeling and the feeling left.

Notice that both of these are the predictable fruit of a single bad theology, the belief that the felt presence of God is the measure of the real presence of God. The whole history of Christian spirituality stands against that belief. The deepest souls in the tradition, the ones who knew God most intimately, are precisely the ones who wrote most about his apparent absence, who insisted that the dark night is not a sign of God's departure but often a sign of his deeper work, who taught that a faith that can only function in the sunlight is a faith that has never been tested and does not yet know whether it loves God or only loves the way God makes it feel. That is the question the dry season exists to ask. Do you love God, or do you love his consolations. Do you want him, or do you want the feeling of him. Most of us cannot answer that honestly until the feeling is taken away.

And the watching skeptic, who has seen plenty of emotional religion, reads the difference. He has watched the enthusiastic believer ride a high and then disappear when life went gray. He has seen faith that was clearly just a mood, here on the mountaintop and gone in the valley. What stops him, when anything does, is the other kind, the believer who keeps showing up to a God who has gone silent, who keeps praying into the dark, who serves and trusts and obeys with no emotional payoff at all, simply because he believes it is true and he has decided to be faithful whether or not he is rewarded with a feeling. That is not religion as therapy. That is something the skeptic cannot easily explain, a love that persists past the point where it stopped being pleasant, and it is one of the few things that looks, to a watching world, like it might actually be real. The dry season, faithfully endured, is an apologetic that no mountaintop experience can match. It is the proof that you wanted God and not just the glow.

parts.title: The Silence That Is Not Absence
parts.body:
Begin with the fact that Scripture is full of the silence, that the Bible does not hide the dry season but puts it at the center, in the mouths of its greatest saints. My God, my God, why have you forsaken me, the psalmist cries in Psalm 22, and Jesus takes that exact cry as his own from the cross. How long, O Lord, will you forget me forever, prays Psalm 13, how long will you hide your face from me. The psalms of lament, which make up a third of the Psalter, are very largely the prayers of people who can no longer feel the God they are praying to, and the staggering thing is that God put them in the prayer book. He authorized the language of his own apparent absence. He gave his people words for the silence, which means the silence is not a failure of faith but a country faith was always meant to be able to cross.

Look at where it shows up. Job, the righteous man, cries out that he goes forward and God is not there, backward and he cannot perceive him, on the left and the right and he cannot find him, and God lets the silence stand for chapter after chapter before he finally speaks. The prophets knew it. Where is the Lord, they ask. Will you hide yourself forever. Even the gap between the testaments, the four hundred years between Malachi and the angel's announcement to Zechariah, is a great silence, a divinely intended drought, and it ends not with an explanation but with the coming of the Word made flesh. The whole biblical pattern teaches that God's silence is real, that it is sometimes long, and that it is never the same as his absence. He was working in the four hundred years of silence. He was working in Job's unanswered chapters. The silence was not nothing. It was a hidden labor.

This is the heart of what the tradition learned to call the dark night of the soul, and the phrase comes from a sixteenth-century Spanish friar named John of the Cross, who wrote the definitive map of the desert. John, imprisoned and afflicted, distinguished two different darknesses that the soul passes through, and the distinction is the most useful thing anyone has ever said about dryness. The first he called the night of the senses, when God withdraws the emotional sweetness of the early Christian life, the feelings and consolations that a young believer leans on. He withdraws them, John said, not as punishment but as weaning, the way a mother weans a child from the breast so that it can eat solid food, because the believer has come to love the consolations more than the God who gave them, and the only way to teach the soul to love God for himself is to take the feelings away and see whether the love remains. The dryness, in other words, is not God leaving. It is God maturing you, dismantling a faith propped up by feeling so that a stronger faith, propped up by nothing but God himself, can be built in its place.

The deeper darkness John called the night of the spirit, a more painful purgation in which God seems to withdraw not just the feelings but himself, in which the soul feels abandoned and even reprobate, and this, John insisted, is the most loving and most fruitful work God does, though it feels like the opposite. In this darkness God is burning away the soul's subtle self-reliance, its hidden pride, its tendency to make even its spiritual life a project of the self, until nothing is left but naked faith, naked hope, naked love, a soul that clings to God for no reason at all except that he is God. John's great insight is that the dark night is the work of God's love precisely when it feels most like his absence, that the deeper the darkness the closer often the labor, that the soul is being carried in exactly the moments it feels most dropped. Faith, he said, is the secret ladder that we climb in the dark.

Ignatius of Loyola, the Spanish soldier turned founder of the Jesuits, gave the church the other essential tool, the discernment of consolation and desolation. In his Spiritual Exercises, written in the 1520s and 1530s, Ignatius taught that the spiritual life moves through times of consolation, when the soul feels the presence and love of God and is drawn toward him, and times of desolation, when it feels dry, distant, tempted, and pulled away. And he gave rules for both, which are pure gold for the dry season. The first rule is the hardest and the most important. In desolation, never make a major change. The voice you hear in the dark is not a reliable guide, and the resolutions you formed in the light still hold. Do not abandon the practice, the commitment, the faith, that you adopted when you could feel God, just because you cannot feel him now. Wait. Hold the line. The desolation will pass, and you will see more clearly on the far side. The second rule is that you must keep doing in the dryness what you did in the consolation, keep praying, keep coming, keep serving, leaning harder rather than less, because the desolation is precisely the test of whether your faith was real or only a feeling. Ignatius understood that desolation is not always God withdrawing for your good. Sometimes it is your own sloth or sin, and sometimes it is spiritual attack, and part of the work is discerning the source. But in every case his counsel is the same. Do not flee. Stand. The feeling lies. The truth holds.

And all of it points to Gethsemane and the cross, where the Son of God himself entered the deepest desolation, sweating blood as he begged for the cup to pass and heard no answer, and then cried from the cross the abandonment of Psalm 22, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me. Here is the staggering center of the Christian faith on the silence. The Father was never closer to the Son than at the cross, was accomplishing in that very darkness the salvation of the world, and the Son could feel none of it. The objective presence and the felt presence came apart entirely, and the love of God was never more fully at work than in the moment it felt most absent. So when you pray into the silence and feel forsaken, you are not somewhere God has never been. You are in the place Christ has already gone before you, and because he was forsaken in fact, you will never be forsaken in fact, however completely you may be forsaken in feeling. The silence that swallowed him means the silence will never finally swallow you. That is the gospel for the dry season. Not that the feeling will return, though often it does, but that the One who endured the real abandonment did so precisely so that yours would only ever be the felt kind, and the felt kind, however dark, is a darkness he is already standing in with you.

parts.title: The Tradition of the Desert
parts.body:
The church has known about spiritual dryness from the beginning, and treated it not as an anomaly but as a regular and even necessary stage of the life with God. The desert fathers of the fourth century, who went into the Egyptian wilderness around the year 300 to seek God in solitude, knew the dry season intimately and gave it a name. They called the worst of it acedia, the noonday demon, the deadly listlessness that descends on the soul in the middle of the day and the middle of the spiritual life, draining prayer of all sweetness, making the cell feel like a prison and God feel like a rumor. Evagrius of Pontus described it with uncanny precision around the year 380, the way it makes the hours crawl, the way it whispers that the spiritual effort is pointless and somewhere else would be better. And their counsel was the counsel of all the tradition that followed. Do not flee the cell. Stay. The demon of acedia is defeated not by escape but by endurance, by remaining in the place and the practice when every feeling says abandon them.

The contemplative tradition built on this for a thousand years. The anonymous English author of The Cloud of Unknowing, writing around 1375, taught that God is often met precisely in a darkness, a cloud of unknowing, where the feelings and even the thoughts fall silent and the soul reaches toward God in naked love alone. This was not a problem to be solved but a higher country to be entered, the place where the soul stops grasping God with its faculties and simply holds to him in trust. Julian of Norwich, around 1393, wrote of the alternation of what she called weal and woe, the times of felt comfort and the times of desolation, and concluded that both are gifts of the same loving God, that he gives the comfort to draw us and permits the desolation to deepen us, and that through it all, all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well.

The Spanish mystics brought the map to its fullest development in the sixteenth century. Teresa of Avila, in her Interior Castle of 1577, charted the soul's passage through successive rooms toward union with God and was unflinching about the long dry stretches and the trials that each stage required, the times when prayer is nothing but distraction and dust. Her friend and fellow reformer John of the Cross gave the desert its enduring name and its theology in the Dark Night of the Soul, written after his own imprisonment in 1577 and 1578, and his insistence that the darkness is the inflowing of God, painful only because the soul is not yet purified enough to receive the light without pain, has comforted desperate believers for four centuries. The whole Carmelite tradition treated the dark night not as a sign of God's displeasure but as one of the most intimate works of his love.

And the dryness was no respecter of greatness. The closer the saint, the more the tradition found, the darker the nights could be. In our own time the letters of Mother Teresa of Calcutta, published after her death in 2007, revealed that this woman who radiated the love of Christ to the dying poor of Calcutta lived for nearly fifty years in an almost unbroken spiritual darkness, feeling no presence of the God she served with everything she had, writing of a silence and emptiness so great that she looked and did not find him, listened and did not hear him. And she kept serving. She kept praying into the void. She decided, as her spiritual directors helped her see, that her very darkness was a participation in the thirst and abandonment of Christ on the cross, that she could love him in the dark by sheer faithful will when she could not feel him at all. Her hidden life is perhaps the most powerful testimony the modern church has to the truth the whole tradition guarded, that the felt absence of God and his real absence are not the same, and that some of his most beloved children serve him their whole lives long in a silence that turns out, on the far side, to have been a fullness all along.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: The dry season touches places where spirituality, psychology, and the body overlap, and honest secular observers have learned real things about the inner life that the church is foolish to ignore. All truth is God's truth. What follows takes five bodies of secular insight seriously, names what each sees clearly, and tests each against Scripture, because every account of the empty inner life carries a hidden picture of what the human person is and what the emptiness means, and the picture is where the wisdom is won or lost.

secular.author: Andrew Solomon, The Noonday Demon
secular.whatItGetsRight: Solomon and the science of depression describe with painful accuracy the way the illness flattens everything, drains color from experience, makes love and meaning and even prayer feel hollow and unreachable, and does so for reasons that are often biological rather than spiritual or moral. Crucially, it names that this flatness is not chosen, not a failure of will or faith, and that no amount of trying harder will lift it, because the machinery of feeling itself has gone dark. This is a vital corrective to a church that too often spiritualizes what is actually an illness.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The clinical account is a true and merciful description of one cause of inner deadness and must never be overridden by piety, and Scripture has no quarrel with it. Where it stops short is meaning. Medicine can name the chemistry and treat it, thank God, and it cannot tell you whether your dark valley has any significance at all, whether anyone is in it with you, whether it leads anywhere. Scripture does not deny the biology and adds what the biology cannot reach, that even a depression endured in faith is not meaningless, that the God who feels absent is present, that the valley has a far side. The wisdom of the dry season is precisely to discern which deadness is illness, to be treated, and which is the soul's purgation, to be endured, and often it is both at once.

secular.source: The psychology of habituation and hedonic adaptation
secular.author: Research on the hedonic treadmill, Brickman and Campbell
secular.whatItGetsRight: Psychologists have shown that human beings adapt to repeated pleasures, that the feeling produced by any experience fades with repetition as the nervous system adjusts to a new baseline, which is why the thrill of a new car or a new relationship or a new spiritual experience inevitably dims. This explains a great deal of the early-faith glow and its fading. The feelings of the new convert were always going to habituate, not because anything went wrong but because that is how feeling works in a body.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The science accurately describes why feelings fade and wrongly implies that the fading is all there is, that beneath the adapting nervous system there is no deeper reality being revealed. Scripture agrees that the early consolations naturally diminish and reads the diminishing very differently, as the providential weaning John of the Cross described, an opportunity for love to grow up past its dependence on feeling. Where habituation theory sees only a nervous system returning to baseline, Scripture sees God using the very fading to ask whether you wanted him or only the glow, and to build a faith that no longer needs the feeling to stand. The mechanism is real. The meaning the mechanism is being used to accomplish is what the science cannot see.

secular.author: Steven Hayes and the ACT tradition
secular.whatItGetsRight: This therapeutic approach teaches that you can act according to your deepest values even when your feelings do not cooperate, that emotions need not drive behavior, and that a person can keep doing what matters in the presence of discomfort, dryness, and the absence of motivation. This is genuinely close to the wisdom of Ignatius, who taught that in desolation you keep doing what you committed to in consolation, that you do not let the feeling govern the action. The insight that faithfulness can run ahead of feeling is a real and useful recovery.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The therapy rightly separates action from feeling and grounds the action in nothing more than self-chosen values. Scripture grounds the same persistence in something far sturdier, in the objective faithfulness of a God who is present whether or not he is felt, so that holding the line in the dark is not merely an act of personal integrity but a real relationship with a real Person who is holding you back. ACT can teach you to keep moving toward your values in the fog. It cannot tell you that there is Someone in the fog with you, that the darkness has a far side, or that your faithfulness is being met by a faithfulness greater than your own. The technique is a true echo of Ignatius without the Lord who makes Ignatius make sense.

secular.author: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi and the psychology of optimal experience
secular.whatItGetsRight: This research illuminates the conditions under which human beings experience deep absorption, joy, and a sense of transcendence, and helps explain why certain practices and settings reliably produce felt closeness and others do not. It rightly observes that such peak states are real, valuable, and also intermittent, that no one lives on the mountaintop, and that the pursuit of constant peak experience is self-defeating. This is useful for understanding the early raptures of faith and their natural intermittency.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The research describes the conditions of felt transcendence accurately and treats the peak experience as the thing itself, the summit to be sought. Scripture warns against exactly that, against making the experience the goal, against loving the consolations of God more than the God of the consolations. The dry season is in large part God's correction of a faith that had begun to chase the peak. Csikszentmihalyi can help you understand why the worship high faded and how it might be induced again. Scripture asks a more searching question, whether you are willing to follow God down off the mountain into the long flat country where most of the real walking is done, and to love him there, where there is no flow at all.

secular.source: Existential psychology and the experience of meaninglessness
secular.author: Viktor Frankl, Man's Search for Meaning
secular.whatItGetsRight: Frankl, writing from the death camps, observed that human beings can endure almost any suffering, including the suffering of apparent meaninglessness and abandonment, if they can find or hold a meaning within it, and that the will to meaning can sustain a person through a darkness that destroys those who have nothing to hold. This speaks directly to the dry season, where the temptation is to conclude that the silence means nothing and therefore everything is pointless. Frankl's witness that meaning can be held even in the abyss is profound and hard-won.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Frankl rightly sees that a person can endure the void if they can hold a meaning in it, and locates that meaning finally in the will of the sufferer, in the stance the person takes. Scripture locates it outside the sufferer entirely, in a God who is present in the darkness whether or not the sufferer can construct any meaning at all. This matters most precisely when the strength to make meaning fails, when the dry season has drained even the will to hold on. Frankl's meaning depends on the sufferer's capacity to supply it. The gospel's hope depends on nothing in the sufferer, only on the faithfulness of the One who was himself forsaken so that the forsaken would never finally be alone. When you cannot make meaning, Christ is still there. That is the one thing Frankl's brave humanism cannot promise.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Christians who hold the same Scripture and have walked the same desert still differ about how to read the dry season, and the difference is genuinely pastoral, because reading it wrong does real harm. It runs to the question of how often spiritual dryness is a purifying work of God to be endured and how often it is a sign of something gone wrong, in the soul or the body, to be addressed. Hear each view at its strongest, because both are trying to care faithfully for suffering people and both are guarding against a real and dangerous error.

views.view: Dryness is usually God's purifying work, to be endured in faith
views.body: This view, rooted in the contemplative tradition of John of the Cross and Ignatius, reads the dry season chiefly as a normal and even precious stage of spiritual growth, the dark night through which God matures a soul that had grown too dependent on feeling. It counsels patience, perseverance, and trust above all, urging the dry believer not to panic, not to abandon the practices, not to go hunting for a problem to fix, but to wait on God in the darkness and to receive the desert as the gift it secretly is. Advocates warn that the modern instinct to immediately pathologize or troubleshoot every dry season can rob the soul of the very purgation God intends, that a believer rushed toward a feeling, a technique, or a treatment may never learn the deeper faithfulness that only the long endurance teaches. They point to the cloud of witnesses, to Mother Teresa's fifty years of darkness borne in faithful service, as proof that the most fruitful Christian life is often the driest, and that the impulse to escape the desert is frequently the very impulse God is trying to crucify. The danger they are guarding against is real, a shallow and anxious Christianity that treats every absence of feeling as an emergency, that cannot tolerate spiritual silence, that medicates or entertains away the holy darkness through which God does his deepest work, and so produces souls that never grow past the milk of early consolation into the solid food of mature faith. Against that, they hold that the desert is to be walked, not fled, and that the believer who endures the silence in trust will find on the far side a God he loves for himself and not for his gifts.

views.view: Dryness has many causes, and discernment and care must come first
views.body: This view honors the contemplative tradition and insists that it must not become a blanket diagnosis, because not every dry season is a dark night and treating them all as purgation can be cruel. It points out that the same flatness in prayer can be caused by depression, by exhaustion, by unconfessed sin, by trauma, by grief, by a body that is simply ill, and that to tell a clinically depressed believer to embrace the holy darkness is to leave him drowning while calling it sanctification. Advocates urge careful discernment of the source, attention to the whole person including the body, and a readiness to name when what looks spiritual is actually medical or relational or circumstantial. They point to the wisdom that grace perfects nature and does not bypass it, that the God who made the body works through rest and food and friendship and, when needed, through doctors and counselors, and that there is no more shame in treating a depression than in setting a broken bone. The danger they are guarding against is also real and grievous, a spiritualizing piety that romanticizes suffering it should be relieving, that praises the dark night while a brother sinks into untreated illness, that mistakes a treatable condition for a mystical gift and so withholds the very help God has provided. Against that, they hold that love demands discernment, that the first question in any dry season is not which spiritual posture to adopt but what is actually going on, and that genuine faith makes full and unashamed use of every means of grace God has given, the medical and the relational no less than the contemplative.

parts.title: What the Desert Forms in a Person
parts.body:
The dry season, faithfully endured, forms things in a soul that the sunlit season never could, and this is the secret the tradition guards most carefully, that the desert is not wasted ground but the very place God does his deepest building. The believer who walks through the silence and keeps believing comes out changed, and the change is not visible in the moment and not measurable by feeling, which is exactly why it is the kind of change that lasts.

The desert forms a faith that no longer depends on feeling, which is the only kind of faith that can be trusted. As long as you can feel God, you do not know whether you love him or love the feeling, and neither do you. The dryness settles the question. The believer who keeps coming to a silent God, who prays into the dark with no emotional payoff, who serves and trusts when there is nothing in it for him to feel, has been given a faith that stands on God himself and not on the weather of his own heart. This faith is unshakable in a way the feeling faith never was, because it has already survived the loss of everything that propped it up, and there is nothing left to take away.

The desert forms humility, the deep kind that comes from the loss of spiritual self-reliance. In the consolations a believer can mistake his own warmth for spiritual attainment, can quietly congratulate himself on his closeness to God, can build a hidden pride out of his experiences. The dry season strips all of that away. The soul in the desert has nothing to boast of, no glow to point to, no sense of progress, and is thrown back entirely on the bare mercy of God. John of the Cross said this was the whole point of the night of the spirit, the burning away of a subtle spiritual pride that no other fire could reach, and the soul that submits to it emerges purified of a self-congratulation it did not even know it had.

The desert forms compassion, the costly kind that can sit with another person in the dark without rushing to fix it. The believer who has walked through his own dry season cannot any longer offer the cheap comfort that only works in the sunlight. He knows too much. He has felt the silence himself, and so he can be present to the friend in the desert without panicking, without spiritualizing, without the false cheer that wounds the suffering. The dry season makes a person safe for other sufferers, which is a gift the church desperately needs and only the tested can give.

And the desert forms a love that wants God for himself. This is the final and the deepest formation, the thing the whole night exists to produce. As long as the consolations flow, the soul is always at risk of loving the gifts more than the Giver, of using God for the warmth he provides. The desert removes the warmth and asks the searching question, and the soul that keeps loving God when there is nothing in it for the feelings has been brought to the purest love a creature can offer, a love that wants God not for what he gives but simply because he is God. This is what the saints came back from the desert carrying. Not a restored feeling, though often that returned too, but something better, a love that had been refined in the fire until it was finally and fully real, a love that could say with Job, though he slay me, yet will I trust him, and mean it, because it had already trusted him through the long dark when there was no reason left to trust but God himself.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: The dry season is not escaped by technique, and anyone who promises to restore the feeling in five steps has not understood the desert. But it can be walked faithfully, and there are practices that keep a soul steady in the dark and let God do his hidden work. None of what follows will manufacture the presence you have lost, and that is not the goal. The goal is to remain faithful in the silence until the silence has done its work. Begin where you are, with one thing, this week. And hear this clearly, because it matters most. If the flatness extends to all of life, if you have lost interest in everything and not only in prayer, if you cannot sleep or cannot stop sleeping, if hope itself has gone, this may be depression, a real and treatable illness, and the most spiritual thing you can do is see a doctor. Seeking that help is not a failure of faith. It is faith using the means God has provided.

steps: Name what you are in, gently and without panic. Ask whether this is most likely God's purifying dryness, or exhaustion, or grief, or unconfessed sin, or depression. You do not have to know for certain. Just begin to discern, because the right response depends on the cause, and naming it is the first step out of the fog.

Pray the psalms of lament when you have no words of your own. Pray Psalm 13, Psalm 22, Psalm 88. God put these in the prayer book for exactly this season. When you cannot generate a prayer, borrow one, and let the inspired words carry you when your own heart is mute.

Take Ignatius's first rule and make no major spiritual change. Do not quit the church, abandon the practice, or rewrite your faith in the dark. The resolutions you made in the light still hold. Whatever you decide, decide it later, on the far side, when you can see.

Tell one trusted person the truth. Break the loneliness of performing a closeness you do not feel. Say to a wise friend or a pastor, God feels absent and I do not know why. The silence grows heavier in secret and lighter when it is shared with someone who will not flinch.

Keep doing in the dryness what you did in the consolation. Keep showing up to prayer, to Scripture, to worship, to the table, even when you feel nothing. This is Ignatius's hardest rule and his most important one. You are leaning harder, not less, and the faithfulness itself is the prayer when the feeling is gone.

Lower the bar and shorten the practice. In a dry season, a long heroic devotional regimen often makes things worse. Pray one honest sentence. Read one verse. Light a candle and sit in silence for five minutes. Faithfulness in the desert is measured in steadiness, not intensity.

Read someone who has been here. Take up John of the Cross, or the letters of Mother Teresa, or a good book on the dark night, and let the cloud of witnesses tell you that this country has been crossed before by people who loved God deeply. You are not the first, and you are not faithless.

Tend the body, because the body and the soul are not separable. Get the sleep, take the walk, eat the food, see the friend. Much spiritual dryness lifts when the exhausted body is finally rested, and grace works through ordinary means more often than through dramatic ones.

Get help discerning the cause, with someone wiser than you. Sit with a seasoned pastor or spiritual director and let them help you read your own desert. Is this purgation to be endured, or a problem to be addressed, or both. You cannot easily diagnose yourself in the dark, and you were not meant to walk this alone.

If the signs point to depression, see a doctor, and do it without shame. Persistent loss of all joy, of sleep, of hope, of the will to live, is not a spiritual failure to pray away. It is an illness God can heal through medical means, and seeking that help is an act of faith, not its abandonment.

Build a rule of life that does not depend on feeling. Set fixed times and simple practices that you keep regardless of your emotional weather, so that your faith runs on commitment rather than on mood. The believers who survive long deserts are the ones whose practice was never built on the feeling in the first place.

Look for God in the dark in new places, not the old ones. He is often present in the desert in the love of friends, in the beauty of the ordinary, in acts of service, in the bread and wine, even when he is silent in your private prayer. Stop demanding he show up only where he used to, and watch for where he actually is.

Let the desert do its work of purifying your love. Stop measuring your faith by your feelings, this year and for the rest of your life, and let God use the dryness to build a love that wants him for himself. The goal was never the restoration of the glow. The goal is a faith that stands on God alone.

Become a companion for others in the dark. Use what the desert taught you to sit with other dry souls without panic or false cheer. The believer who has crossed the silence is one of the few people safe enough to walk another through it, and the church is starving for that kind of company.

Hold the long view that the tradition holds. The dry season is a stage and not a destination, and the God who feels absent is working in the silence as surely as he worked in the four hundred years before Christ came. Trust the hidden labor. The far side is real, and many have reached it.

Anchor everything in Gethsemane and the cross. When the silence is deepest, remember that the Son of God entered it first, was forsaken in fact so that you would only ever be forsaken in feeling, and was never closer to the Father than in the darkness where he could feel nothing. You are not somewhere Christ has never been. You are standing where he stood, which means even your darkest silence is a darkness he is in with you, and on the far side of his is resurrection.
